implementation_notes: C++ has no standard breaker, so this is the classic hand-written realization: a std::atomic state (or a mutex-protected copy), atomic counters or a small mutex-guarded window, and std::chrono::steady_clock for both the cooldown deadline and slow-call detection. Admission is a single atomic load on the hot path - closed returns immediately, open compares the deadline and compare-exchanges into half-open - which is what keeps the breaker cheaper than the call it protects; the protected call stays outside any lock. There is nothing to replace the structure with, so the classic form is always justified; the design decision is which parts stay lock-free (state reads, counters) and which are serialized (transitions, window updates).
pitfalls: Using std::chrono::system_clock for the cooldown: it can jump backwards and keep the circuit open (or closed) for the wrong duration; use steady_clock.
A per-call CAS loop on shared counters turns the breaker into a contention point under high concurrency; keep the hot path to a single atomic load and batch or shard the counter updates.
std::atomic does not make the whole transition atomic: state and counters need deliberate acquire/release ordering, or a thread can admit a call against a stale state.
A breaker held by value in a policy object is copied, and each copy keeps its own counters, so the trip threshold is never reached.

variants.name: Asio-integrated breaker: strand-owned state + steady_timer cooldown (C++17)
variants.implementation_notes: When the client is already Asio-based, the breaker lives in the same executor as the connection: state is owned by the strand (or by a single-threaded io_context) instead of atomics, admission is an ordinary function call on that strand, and the open-to-half-open transition is scheduled with a boost::asio::steady_timer rather than computed lazily on the next call - so recovery starts on time even when traffic is quiet, which is the reason to prefer this variant in event-driven servers. Completion handlers must record success or failure back on the same strand, the timer must outlive its wait, and a cancelled wait completes with operation_aborted, which is not a failure to count. Choose this over the atomic variant when timing accuracy of the half-open transition matters or when the whole client is already callback/coroutine based.
pitfalls: A cancelled timer completes with operation_aborted; counting that as a failure corrupts the statistics whenever the wait is re-armed or the service shuts down.
Without a strand (or a single-threaded io_context) the state becomes a data race, because handlers may run on any thread that runs the context.
The timer must outlive its pending wait: destroying a breaker with an async_wait outstanding leaves a dangling handler.
Blocking work inside a completion handler stalls the whole io_context and hides the dependency's slowness from both the breaker and the timeout.
